name: Bolivar-North Chimborazo Highland Quichua
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Beukema, Ronald W. 1975. A Grammatical Sketch of Chimborazo Quichua. Yale dissertation; also Naula Gaucho & Burns 1975 Bosquejo gramatical del quichua de Chimborazo. Neither online.

new_statements.quote: Quichua essentially has no suprasegmental* phonemes*: unlike Spanish and English, phonetic* stress or accent is almost entirely predictable, falling in almost all cases on the penultimate (next to last) syllable, and does not need to be written[23]. [fn.23:] There is one very small exception to this rule, in which the accent shifts to the final syllable on the last word in the sentence in some cases, but this does not negate the general fact that accent is not phonemic* in Quichua on individual words like it is in Spanish or English. [...] [p.39:] Stress in Quichua is non-phonemic*, and always falls on the penultimate syllable.
new_statements.citation: Aschmann, Richard P. 2020 [2019]. Reference Grammar of Ecuadorian Quichua / Gramática de referencia del quichua ecuatoriano. Edition of 23-oct-2020. Quichua.net.
new_statements.locator: §4.1 'Phonemes of Ecuadorian Quichua', p.20 with footnote 23 (PDF p.22); restated §4.1.4.1.5, p.39 (PDF p.41)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; in Central Highland (Chimborazo) Quichua certain sentence-final focus/topic enclitics (-cá 'and what about', and a related sentence-focus suffix) attract stress to the final syllable of the last word of the sentence.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) Sentence-final shift of accent to the final syllable on the last word in some cases (e.g. ¿Cancá? 'and you?', -cá topic suffix usually stressed; another sentence-focus suffix 'normally has the accent on the final syllable in Central Highland Quichua'); (ii) in Imbabura and Upper Napo (not CHQ) phrase-terminator suffixes may be treated as separate words for accent (chaipica = [čɑypíkɑ] in CHQ but [čɑ́ypikɑ] in Imbabura); (iii) in Lowland Quichua consonant loss between the last two vowels leaves accent in its historical (now non-penultimate) position. Ross (Lesson 1 §2) adds that accent may be shifted to the final syllable 'for added emphasis', marked with a written accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule (each word penultimate); the exception is explicitly sentence-level (last word of the sentence, sentence-final enclitics). Phonetic transcriptions given are Central Highland Quichua citation forms (bɑ́tʸɑ, úsyɑ, púɣyu, kɑwsɑ́yyux). Corroborated first-hand by Ross 1963/2017 Lesson 1 §2 p.1-3: 'Quichua word accent is very regular, falling as a general rule on the penult (second-last syllable) of each word' (aLLIlla, CANgui, alliLLAchu, Ari), based on Colta, Chimborazo.
new_statements.identity_note: Aschmann's grammar covers all Ecuadorian Quichua varieties comparatively but defines 'Central Highland Quichua (CHQ)' as the Quichua of Chimborazo Province (except the extreme south, which is Cañar Quichua, cana1260), much of Cotopaxi, Bolívar and parts of Tungurahua (excluding Salasaka, sala1272) — i.e. Ethnologue qug / Glottolog chim1302 'Bolivar-North Chimborazo Highland Quichua'; the stress statement is given for Quichua generally with CHQ phonetic forms, and the noted Imbabura (imba1240) and Lowland exceptions explicitly do not apply to CHQ. Ross's lessons are based specifically on Colta, Chimborazo Province speech (1958-59), squarely chim1302.

sources.note: §4.1 p.20: Quichua has essentially no suprasegmental phonemes; stress is almost entirely predictable, penultimate in almost all cases; fn.23: small exception where accent shifts to the final syllable of the last word of the sentence; §4.1.4.1.5 p.39: 'Stress in Quichua is non-phonemic, and always falls on the penultimate syllable', with Central Highland Quichua phonetic forms (bɑ́tʸɑ, úsyɑ, púɣyu...); pp. 5.4.5.2.1.1.1.3 etc.: sentence-final -cá and another sentence-focus suffix carry final accent in Central Highland Quichua.

sources.citation: Ross, Ellen M. 2017 [orig. 1963, Introduction to Ecuador Highland Quichua]. Introduction to Central Highland Quichua of Ecuador, or Quichua in Ten Easy Lessons. Vol. 1 (Lessons 1-25). Revised and translated into Spanish by Richard P. Aschmann. Quichua.net.
sources.note: Lesson 1 §2 'Word accent' (p.1-3, PDF p.15): 'Quichua word accent is very regular, falling as a general rule on the penult (second-last syllable) of each word' (aLLIlla, CANgui, alliLLAchu, Ari); for added emphasis the accent may shift to the final syllable, written with an accent mark; Lesson 2 note 2 (p.2-3): final accent in '¿Cancá?'. Based on Chimborazo (Colta) Quichua learned 1958-59.
